DEPARTMENT 732 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 24STC29859    Hearing Date: August 7, 2026    Dept: 732

L.A. Commercial Group, Inc. v. Associated Construction, LLC, et al. 

 

Friday, August 7, 2024 

 

 

 

CASE NUMBER: 24STC29859 

 

UNOPPOSED 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Attorney Simrandeep S. Tiwana Motion to Be Relieved as Counsel 

 ___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Facts: Plaintiff L.A. Commercial Group, Inc. dba Continental Commercial Group seeks to collect from Defendant Associated Construction, LLC on an assigned debt of $364,328.51 from National Ready Mixed Concrete Company. 

Procedural History: On November 13, 2024, Plaintiff filed a form complaint for common counts, and breach of contract. On February 11, 2025, the court entered a default judgment for $383,260.21. On May 20, 2025, the court entered the parties’ stipulation to set aside the default judgment and writ of execution. Defendant answered the complaint on June 6, 2025. 

On October 7, 2025, current counsel substituted into the action.  

On July 10, 2026, the court continued the June 5, 2026, filed motion to be relived as counsel to August 7, 2026, in order to allow for supplemental briefing regarding the basis for withdrawal. 

Analysis 

  1. RELIEVED AS COUNSEL 

Code of Civil Procedure § 284 states that “[t]he attorney in an action or special proceeding may be changed at any time before or after judgment or final determination” upon either consent of both client and attorney, or “[u]pon order of the court, upon the application of either client or attorney, after notice from one to the other..” (Code Civ. Proc. § 284, subd. (b).) California Rule of Court (“CRC”) Rule 3.1362 states the requirements for a motion to be relieved as counsel under Code of Civil Procedure § 284. No memorandum is required (CRC Rule 3.1362, subd. (b)), but the motion must be accompanied by (1) a declaration stating why a motion has been brought instead of filing a consent (without compromising attorney-client confidentiality) (CRC Rule 3.1362, subd. (c)); (2) proof of service of the motion (CRC Rule 3.1362, subd. (d); and (3) all hearing dates scheduled in the action or proceeding, including the date of trial. (CRC Rule 3.1362, subd. (e).) “The proposed order relieving counsel must be prepared on the Order Granting Attorney's Motion to Be Relieved as Counsel--Civil (form MC-053) and must be lodged with the court with the moving papers.” (Ibid.)  

 

In continuing the prior order, the court wrote in relevant part: “The present motion pertains to Simrandeep S. Tiwana, of the firm Meyers Nave, counsel for Defendant Associated Construction, LLC. The motion is supported by a declaration of counsel, who states that permissive withdrawal is appropriate under California Rules of Professional Conduct, Rule 1.16, subd. (b)(4), (5), and (10), which pertain to situations in which the client makes it unreasonably difficult to carry out the representation, the client breaches a material term of the agreement, or the attorney believes the tribunal granting permission to withdraw will find good cause therefore. (Tiwana Decl. Att. 2.) The motion includes a proof of service and a proposed order form listing upcoming dates of hearing. Trial is set for October 26, 2027.” 

 

“Counsel does not set forth sufficient grounds to grant the requested relief. The supporting declaration includes no factual information. It cites certain grounds for permissive withdrawal within the Rules of Professional Conduct, including a catchall provision, and states that the attorney seeks relief under these grounds. This is insufficient, as the declaration does not state even in “general terms” why the present motion is brought in lieu of a voluntary substitution. (CRC Rule 3.1362, subd. (c).)” 

 

Counsel appears to have also reserved a second motion though only seeks the same relief. The court consolidates both reserved motions into a single order. 

On July 24, 2026, Counsel filed a pleading paper formatted “Notice of Hearing on Motion to Be Relieved as Counsel,” and “Declaration of Simran S. Tiwana.” The July 24, 2026, “notice of hearing” and “declaration,” are not filed on the MC-051 and MC-052 forms. The new papers lack any copy of an order on form MC-053. The new papers include the prior court ruling indicating counsel’s presumed reliance on the prior filed application. To the extent Counsel tried to refile and supersede the prior motion, the new pleadings violate all statutory requirements. 

The revised notice and declaration were served by email on July 22, 2026—16 calendar days from the date of the hearing. The motion must be served 16 court days (July 15, 2026) from the date of the hearing. (Code Civ. Proc., §1005, subd. (b).) The 16 days before the hearing also fails to add in the required two additional days for email service. It also remains unstated whether the client agreed to email service. (Code Civ. Proc., §1010.6.) Regardless of a new motion, or notice of a new hearing date of the prior motion as ordered by the court, the notice or new motion are untimely.  

 

Accordingly, the single motion is CONTINUED to permit counsel Simrandeep S. Tiwana to present a timely served, form compliant motion, including a declaration incorporated into the MC-052 form, the “general terms” allowing for relief, and order with all updated hearing date information. The court directs counsel to not reserve a third new date for the next hearing. 

 

Dated: August 7, 2026

Hon. Richard Kemalyan 

Judge of the Superior Court 

 

Case Number: 25STC16447    Hearing Date: August 7, 2026    Dept: 732

John Devenanzio v. David Miklofsky, et al. 

 

Friday, August 7, 2024 

 

 

 

CASE NUMBER: 25STC16447 

 

UNOPPOSED 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Defendants David Milklosfsy and TheCombined, LLC’s Motion for Pro Hac Vice Admission of Moshe Y. Warga 

 ___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Facts: Plaintiff John Devenanzio alleges Defendant David Milklosfsy worked with Plaintiff as both a business manager and agent. Plaintiff alleges Milklosfsy improperly/prematurely collected certain commissions/fees and transferred them to Defendant TheCombined, LLC. Plaintiff also alleges Defendants hold certain access information for six (6) Bitcoins owned by Plaintiff, and refuses to turnover access. 

Procedural History: On November 13, 2024, Plaintiff filed a 13 cause of action complaint:   

1. Breach Of Fiduciary Duty  

2. Conversion  

3. Unjust Enrichment  

4. Constructive Trust  

5. Resulting Trust  

6. Civil Theft  

7. Negligence 8. Breach Of Contract  

9. Promissory Estoppel  

10. Intentional Misrepresentation  

11. Negligent Misrepresentation  

12. Constructive Fraud  

13. Accounting 

 

On March 20, 2026, David Milklosfsy answered and filed a cross-complaint against John Devenanzio for six causes of action:  

 

1. Breach Of Contract 

2. Breach Of Implied Contract 

3. Promissory Estoppel  

4. Intentional Misrepresentation  

5. Negligent Misrepresentation  

6. Unjust Enrichment 

 

Analysis 

  1. PRO HAC VICE 

Pro hac vice admission in California is governed by California Rules of Court, Rule 9.40.  To be admitted pro hac vice, one must be “a member in good standing of and eligible to practice before the bar of any United States court or the highest court in any state, territory, or insular possession of the United States.”  (California Rules of Court, rule 9.40(a).)  However, in no case shall an attorney appear pro hac vice if the attorney is a resident of California, regularly employed in California, or “regularly engaged in substantial business, professional, or other activities in the State of California.” 

 

An attorney seeking pro hac vice admission must file a verified application in both court and the State Bar of California establishing: 

 

(1) [t]he applicant's residence and office address; (2)[t]he courts to which the applicant has been admitted to practice and the dates of admission; (3)[t]hat the applicant is a member in good standing in those courts; (4)[t]hat the applicant is not currently suspended or disbarred in any court; (5)[t]he title of court and cause in which the applicant has filed an application to appear as counsel¿pro hac vice¿in this state in the preceding two years, the date of each application, and whether or not it was granted; and (6)[t]he name, address, and telephone number of the active member of the State Bar of California who is attorney of record. (California Rules of Court, rule 9.40(d).) 

 

The application of Moshe Y. Warga complies with California Rules of Court, Rule 9.40. Warga was granted pro hac vice appearance privileges in one other case in Broward County Florida [Declaration of Moshe Warga.] The application includes representation of payment to the California State Bar. [Declaration of Chaim Gordon.] 

 

Accordingly, the motion is GRANTED. 

 

Dated: August 7, 2026

Case Number: 26STC04819    Hearing Date: August 7, 2026    Dept: 732

UMG Recordings, Inc. v. Mark Opitz 

 

Friday, August 7, 2024 

 

 

 

CASE NUMBER: 26STC04819 

 

UNOPPOSED 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Plaintiff UMG Recordings, Inc.’s Motion for Pro Hac Vice Admission of Richard Mandel 

 ___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Facts: On March 20, 1989, Plaintiff UMG Recordings, Inc. (UMG) predecessor in interest MCA Records, Inc., allegedly entered into a contract with third party Jost Productions, Inc. (Jost) for provision of recording services to band/artist Red Alert, later known as Steelheart. The agreement required Jost to produce a record(s) on behalf of Steelheart. All responsibilities for recording, including payment for the hiring of any and all required personnel were the responsibility of Jost.  

Jost hired Defendant Mark Opitz as a producer. Opitz made a claim for producer royalty payments to which UMG denies any obligation pursuant to the terms of the Jost Productions agreement.  

The second cause of action involves Opitz’s work as a producer with the band INXS. Plaintiff maintains Opitz submitted an improper demand for royalty payment to which Plaintiff maintains no responsibility under a licensing agreement for the use of certain master recordings.  

Procedural History:  

On February 13, 2026, Plaintiff filed a 2 cause of action complaint:   

1. Declaratory Relief (Steelheart)  

2. Declaratory Relief (INXS) 

 

On March 5, 2026, Plaintiff filed an executed Notice of Acknowledgment and Receipt from Defendant. 

 

On July 24, 2026, Defendant, in pro per, from Australia, filed a cross-complaint for  

(I) Accounting 

(2) Breach Of Contract As Intended Third-Party Beneficiary 

(3) Breach Of Implied-In-Fact Contract 

(4) Restitution / Quasi-Contract 

(5) Declaratory Relief 

(6) Account Stated 

 

On July 20, 2026, Plaintiff, in pro per and from Australia, filed an answer. 

Analysis 

  1. PRO HAC VICE 

Pro hac vice admission in California is governed by California Rules of Court, Rule 9.40.  To be admitted pro hac vice, one must be “a member in good standing of and eligible to practice before the bar of any United States court or the highest court in any state, territory, or insular possession of the United States.”  (California Rules of Court, rule 9.40(a).)  However, in no case shall an attorney appear pro hac vice if the attorney is a resident of California, regularly employed in California, or “regularly engaged in substantial business, professional, or other activities in the State of California.” 

 

An attorney seeking pro hac vice admission must file a verified application in both court and the State Bar of California establishing: 

 

(1) [t]he applicant's residence and office address; (2)[t]he courts to which the applicant has been admitted to practice and the dates of admission; (3)[t]hat the applicant is a member in good standing in those courts; (4)[t]hat the applicant is not currently suspended or disbarred in any court; (5)[t]he title of court and cause in which the applicant has filed an application to appear as counsel¿pro hac vice¿in this state in the preceding two years, the date of each application, and whether or not it was granted; and (6)[t]he name, address, and telephone number of the active member of the State Bar of California who is attorney of record. (California Rules of Court, rule 9.40(d).) 

 

The application of Richard Mandel complies with California Rules of Court, Rule 9.40. Mandel was granted pro hac vice appearance privileges in one other case in the Central District of California. [Declaration of Richard Mandel.] The application includes proof of payment to the California State Bar. [Declaration of Talya Goldfinger.] 

 

Accordingly, the motion is GRANTED.

Case Number: BC561928    Hearing Date: August 7, 2026    Dept: 732

Jane Ramsay v. Robert Weinbach, et al. 

 

Friday, August 7, 2026 

 

 

 

CASE NUMBER: BC561928 

 

UNOPPOSED 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Plaintiff Jane Ramsay’s Motion to Seal Opposition to Motion to Compel Arbitration and Related Exhibits 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Facts: This is an action for fraud and breach of contract. The Complaint alleges as follows. Plaintiff Jane Ramsay (“Plaintiff”) entered into an agreement to invest money into a film production at the solicitation of Defendant Robert Weinbach (“Defendant”), who promised to double her investment. (Complaint ¶¶ 7–8.) This solicitation violated several securities laws, and Plaintiff at the time lacked the mental capacity to enter into the agreement following the death of her mother. (Complaint ¶¶¿10–14.)  

Procedural History: Plaintiff filed the Complaint on October 23, 2014, alleging eight causes of action: 

  1. Intentional Misrepresentation 

  1. Negligent Misrepresentation 

  1. Breach of Contract 

  1. Breach of Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing 

  1. Unjust Enrichment 

  1. Conversion 

  1. Breach of Fiduciary Duty 

  1. Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress 

On June 10, 2015, the court granted Defendants motion to compel arbitration.  

Judgment was entered on July 8, 2015 in favor of Defendants.   

Plaintiff filed the present motion to seal on May 21, 2026. No opposition was filed. On June 23, 2026, the court continued the motion to August 7, 2026.  

Discussion: 

 

  1. MOTIONS TO SEAL 

 

The court may order that a record be filed under seal only if it expressly finds facts that establish: 

 

  1. There exists an overriding interest that overcomes the right of public access to the record;  

 

(2) The overriding interest supports sealing the record; 

 

(3) A substantial probability exists that the overriding interest will be prejudiced if the record is not sealed; 

 

(4) The proposed sealing is narrowly tailored; and 

 

(5) No less restrictive means exist to achieve the overriding interest. 

 

(Cal. Rules Ct., rule 2.550(d).)  

 

A party moving to seal records must make a sufficient evidentiary showing to overcome the presumed right of public access to the documents. (see Huffy Corp. v. Superior Court (2003) 112 Cal.App.4th 97, 108 distinguished on unrelated grounds in Curtis v. Superior Court (2021) 62 Cal.App.5th 453, 471.) 

 

“Although self-represented litigants are not entitled to special treatment, they are entitled to the same treatment as a represented party. ... ‘Trial judges must acknowledge that in propria persona litigants often do not have an attorney's level of knowledge about the legal system and are more prone to misunderstanding the court's requirements.’ (Citation). When one party has counsel and the other does not, the trial court ‘should monitor to ensure the in propria persona litigant is not inadvertently misled, either by the represented party or by the court... [S]pecial care should be used to make sure that verbal instructions given in court and written notices are clear and understandable by a layperson.’” (Petrosyan v. Prince Corp. (2013) 223 Cal.App.4th 587, 594.) 

 

Plaintiff Jane Ramsay (“Plaintiff”) in pro per moves to seal various documents associated with the motion to compel arbitration filed by Defendants Robert Weinbach and Cyclone Productions, Inc. (“Defendants”) on February 23, 2015, and granted by the court on June 10, 2015, more than ten years before the present motion to seal was filed.  

 

Plaintiff argues that her opposition materials, Defendants’ reply materials, and the court’s ruling contain references to a declaration nominally submitted by herself, in which she attests to various internal and external factors that allegedly deprived her of capacity to enter into the investment agreement which is the subject of this action. Plaintiff argues that at least one of the factors identified, referenced in the court’s ruling granting the motion, was a fabrication of her attorney, and that the remaining factors constitute private matters that she had not authorized her attorney to disclose. (Ramsay Decl. ¶¶ 4–15.) Plaintiff contends that these matters intrude upon her privacy and that she is prejudiced by permitting them to remain in a publicly accessible document. (Ramsay Decl. ¶ 10.)  

 

Plaintiff notes that she complained to the California State Bar regarding her former counsel in this matter in 2016, and that the attorney, Michael J. Gulden, was disbarred in 2019. (Ramsay Decl. ¶ 2, Exhs. A, B.) Plaintiff states that she recently reviewed the old declarations in connection with a “new action,” and was shocked to find the misrepresentations and disclosures they contained. (Ramsay Decl. ¶ 8.)  

 

To establish that an overriding interest is sufficient, plaintiff must clearly identify the interest and demonstrate “a substantial probability that it will be prejudiced absent sealing or closure.”  (Universal City Studios, Inc. v. Superior Court (2003) 110 Cal.App.4th 1273, 1283.) Plaintiff has not demonstrated an overriding interest in the bulk of the matters identified. Plaintiff concedes that much of what is contained in her declaration is true, but argues that it consists of items from her private life and medical history not pertinent to the case and serving no purpose but to sensationalize her life. (Ramsay Decl. ¶ 4.) Privacy may indeed furnish a basis for an order sealing records. (See NBC Subsidiary (KNBC-TV), Inc. v. Superior Court (1999) 20 Cal.4th 1178, 1204.) But it is not true that they are irrelevant to the present action, as Plaintiff tendered the issue of her capacity to sign the agreement in both the Complaint (Complaint ¶ 14) and the opposition to the motion to compel arbitration, which was almost entirely based on her lack of capacity to sign the agreement. Plaintiff does not deny tendering the issue of her capacity in this action. As such, the privacy rights she articulates with respect to the present papers were waived even prior to the long delay preceding the present motion. (See People v. Yang (2021) 67 Cal.App.5th 1, 48 [tender of issue waives psychotherapist-patient privilege]; see Evid. Code, § 1016, subd. (a); Vinson v. Superior Court (1987) 43 Cal.3d 833, 840, 848; In re Lifschutz¿(1970) 2 Cal.3d 415, 439; Patterson v. Superior Court¿(1983) 147 Cal.App.3d 927, 930.) 

 

Plaintiff arguably possesses an overriding interest favoring sealing the allegation of drug use contained in her earlier declaration, repeated in other papers, that she now contends was fabricated by her now-disbarred attorney. A false accusation of illicit drug use identified constitutes a defamatory statement the truth of which Plaintiff now denies. (Ramsay Decl. ¶¶ 4–5; See Franklin v. Dynamic Details, Inc. (2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 375, 387.) However, sealing the records identified is not the least restrictive means by which to address the interest that Plaintiff identifies. (Cal. Rules Ct., rule 2.550(d).)  Such interest may be preserved by the filings now in the public record noting Plaintiff’s denial of the allegation, which denial is the only evidence before the court supporting Plaintiff’s proposed sealing of the records.  

 

Finally, seeking relief after the filing of the pleadings and the significant lapse of time presents grounds for a finding of any waiver of the right to try and seal the documents. There is no indication the documents were presented on condition of a pending motion to seal, or otherwise improperly disclosed privileged information. (Savaglio v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. (2007) 149 Cal.App.4th 588, 598-601.) 

 

The motion is therefore DENIED.  

  

 

 

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles

JANE RAMSAY.,

Plaintiff Jane Ramsay’s Motion to Seal Opposition to Motion to Compel Arbitration and Related Exhibits 

 

 

Plaintiff Jane Ramsay’s Motion to Seal Opposition to Motion to Compel Arbitration and Related Exhibits is DENIED.
